steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper showing that adding unbalancedness to neural Monge map estimators improves unpaired domain translation. Cover the OT/Monge map background, why unbalanced OT is needed, our rescaling framework and its experiments (cell trajectories, perturbation responses, image translation with OT flow matching), and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Unpaired domain translation is about transforming data from a source distribution to a target distribution when there are no paired training samples. This is a significant challenge, because the translation between the distributions has to be meaningful and at the same time relevant features of the input have to be kept. There are many ways to define what properties such a transformation should have, but optimal transport (OT) gives a natural framework, since it matches samples across distributions in the most cost-efficient way. When this optimal correspondence can be written as a map, the map is called a Monge map.

Recently many neural parameterizations have been proposed to estimate Monge maps. The earlier estimators were limited to the squared Euclidean distance, and more flexible approaches have been proposed recently. Neural Monge maps have been applied successfully to many domain translation tasks, including computer vision and modeling how cells respond to perturbations.

Optimal transport in its original formulation assumes that the marginal distributions are static. This limits its applications, as it cannot account for [i] outliers and [ii] undesired distribution shifts, for example class imbalance between distributions as visualized in Figure 1. Unbalanced OT (UOT) gets around these limitations by replacing the conservation of mass constraint with a penalization on mass deviations. Unbalancedness in discrete OT has been shown to be practically important in various applications, such as video registration, computer vision, or domain adaptation. The existing methods that estimate neural Monge maps with unbalancedness are limited to specific Monge map estimators and they rely on adversarial training, which we discuss in detail in Section 4.

- Our framework
  - unbalancedness for any Monge map estimator via re-scaling scheme
  - theory: rescale source and target measures accordingly
  - synthetic + real-world data, different estimators
  - developmental single-cell trajectories with ICNN-based estimators (OT-ICNN)
  - cellular responses to perturbations with Monge gap
- OT flow matching
  - OT-FM: simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows, mini-batch OT couplings
  - extend to unbalanced setting: UOT-FM
  - EMNIST digits -> letters: unbalancedness crucial for meaningful matches
  - benchmark OT-FM on unpaired natural image translation: competitive with established methods
  - UOT-FM: [i] better than OT-FM, [ii] preserves input features, lower learned transport cost
  - new principled method for unpaired image translation
- Contributions
  1. efficient algorithm: any balanced Monge map estimator into unbalanced OT framework
  2. theory: Monge map between measures of unequal mass = Monge map between two rescaled measures
  3. better results on three tasks with three estimators: more biologically plausible cell trajectories, better prediction of responses to cancer drugs, preserves input features in image translation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Unpaired domain translation is about transforming data from a source distribution to a target distribution when there are no paired training samples. This is a significant challenge, because the translation between the distributions has to be meaningful and at the same time relevant features of the input have to be kept. There are many ways to define what properties such a transformation should have, but optimal transport (OT) gives a natural framework, since it matches samples across distributions in the most cost-efficient way. When this optimal correspondence can be written as a map, the map is called a Monge map.

Recently many neural parameterizations have been proposed to estimate Monge maps. The earlier estimators were limited to the squared Euclidean distance, and more flexible approaches have been proposed recently. Neural Monge maps have been applied successfully to many domain translation tasks, including computer vision and modeling how cells respond to perturbations.

Optimal transport in its original formulation assumes that the marginal distributions are static. This limits its applications, as it cannot account for [i] outliers and [ii] undesired distribution shifts, for example class imbalance between distributions as visualized in Figure 1. Unbalanced OT (UOT) gets around these limitations by replacing the conservation of mass constraint with a penalization on mass deviations. Unbalancedness in discrete OT has been shown to be practically important in various applications, such as video registration, computer vision, or domain adaptation. The existing methods that estimate neural Monge maps with unbalancedness are limited to specific Monge map estimators and they rely on adversarial training, which we discuss in detail in Section 4.

Because of these limitations, we introduce a new framework that incorporates unbalancedness into any Monge map estimator, based on a re-scaling scheme. We motivate the approach theoretically, by proving that unbalancedness can be incorporated into neural Monge maps by rescaling the source and target measures accordingly. To show that the approach is versatile, we apply it to both synthetic and real-world data with different neural Monge map estimators. We show that incorporating unbalancedness plays a critical role for inferring trajectories in developmental single-cell data with ICNN-based estimators (OT-ICNN) and for predicting cellular responses to perturbations with the Monge gap.

Another way to approximate Monge maps is OT flow matching (OT-FM), which is a simulation-free technique to train continuous normalizing flows that relies on mini-batch OT couplings. Since our method can be applied universally, we can extend OT-FM to the unbalanced setting (UOT-FM). We show that unbalancedness is crucial to get meaningful matches when translating digits to letters in the EMNIST dataset. We also benchmark OT-FM on unpaired natural image translation and show it gets competitive results compared to established methods. UOT-FM also shows the advantages of unbalancedness in image translation, as it [i] improves the overall performance over OT-FM and [ii] helps to preserve relevant input features and lowers the learned transport cost. So UOT-FM is a new principled method for unpaired image translation. To summarize:

- 1. We propose an efficient algorithm that integrates any balanced Monge map estimator into the unbalanced OT framework.

- 2. We verify the approach theoretically by proving that computing a Monge map between measures of unequal mass can be reformulated as computing a Monge map between two rescaled measures.

- 3. We show that incorporating unbalancedness gives better results across three different tasks using three different Monge map estimators. Our approach recovers more biologically plausible cell trajectories and improves the prediction of how cells respond to cancer drugs. Our method also helps preserve relevant input features on unpaired natural image translation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Unpaired domain translation aims to transform data from a source to a target distribution without access to paired training samples. This setting poses the significant challenge of achieving a meaningful translation between distributions while retaining relevant input features. Although there are many ways to define the desired properties of such a transformation, optimal transport (OT) offers a natural framework by matching samples across distributions in the most cost-efficient way. If this optimal correspondence can be formulated as a map, it is known as a Monge map.

Recently, a considerable number of neural parameterizations for estimating Monge maps have been proposed. While earlier estimators were limited to the squared Euclidean distance [1,2,3], more flexible approaches have been proposed recently [4,5,6,7]. Neural Monge maps have been successfully applied to a variety of domain translation tasks, including computer vision [8,5,6,9] and the modeling of cellular responses to perturbations [10].

In its original formulation, optimal transport assumes static marginal distributions. This can limit its applications, as it cannot account for [i] outliers and [ii] undesired distribution shifts, e.g. class imbalance between distributions as visualized in Figure 1. Unbalanced OT (UOT) [11] overcomes these limitations by replacing the conservation of mass constraint with a penalization on mass deviations. The practical importance of unbalancedness in discrete OT has been demonstrated in various applications, e.g. video registration [12], computer vision [13], or domain adaptation [14]. Existing methods for estimating neural Monge maps with unbalancedness [15,16] are limited to specific Monge map estimators and rely on adversarial training; see Section 4 for a detailed discussion.

In light of these limitations, we introduce a new framework for incorporating unbalancedness into any Monge map estimator based on a re-scaling scheme. We motivate our approach theoretically by proving that unbalancedness can be incorporated into neural Monge maps by rescaling the source and target measures accordingly. To validate its versatility, we show the approach is applicable to both synthetic and real-world data using different neural Monge map estimators. We highlight the critical role of unbalancedness for inferring trajectories in developmental single-cell data using ICNN-based estimators (OT-ICNN) [1] and for predicting cellular responses to perturbations with the Monge gap [4].

Monge maps can also be approximated with OT flow matching (OT-FM) [17,18,19], a simulation-free technique for training continuous normalizing flows [20] that relies on mini-batch OT couplings [6,5]. The universal applicability of our method allows us to extend OT-FM to the unbalanced setting (UOT-FM). We demonstrate that unbalancedness is crucial for obtaining meaningful matches when translating digits to letters in the EMNIST dataset [21]. We also benchmark OT-FM on unpaired natural image translation and show that it achieves competitive results compared to established methods. Moreover, UOT-FM shows the advantages of unbalancedness in image translation, as it [i] improves overall performance over OT-FM and [ii] helps to preserve relevant input features while lowering the learned transport cost. This makes UOT-FM a new principled method for unpaired image translation. To summarize:

- 1. We propose an efficient algorithm to integrate any balanced Monge map estimator into the unbalanced OT framework.

- 2. We theoretically verify our approach by proving that computing a Monge map between measures of unequal mass can be reformulated as computing a Monge map between two rescaled measures.

- 3. We demonstrate that incorporating unbalancedness yields better results across three distinct tasks using three different Monge map estimators. Our approach recovers more biologically plausible cell trajectories and improves the prediction of cellular responses to cancer drugs. Furthermore, it helps to preserve relevant input features in unpaired natural image translation.
